scenes.caption: Photo 1903
scenes.text: A pilot project funded by the United Nations Environment Program (UNEP) revealed that in 40 years, the coast to the east of Cotonou had retreated by 400 meters.

scenes.caption: Photo 1910
scenes.text: At the beginning of the 19th century, Cotonou (then spelled "Kutonou") was a small fishing village, and is thought to have been formally founded by King Ghezo of Dahomey in 1830.

scenes.caption: Photo 1915
scenes.text: In 1851 the French Second Republic made a treaty with King Ghezo that allowed them to establish a trading post at Cotonou.

scenes.caption: Photo 1930
scenes.text: The city is cut in two by a canal, the lagoon of Cotonou, dug by the French in 1855.

scenes.caption: Photo 1930
scenes.text: During the reign of King Glele (1858–89), the territory was ceded to the Second French Empire by a treaty signed in 1878.

scenes.caption: Photo 1930
scenes.text: After Glele's death in 1889, King Béhanzin unsuccessfully tried to challenge the treaty.

scenes.caption: Photo 1930
scenes.text: The town grew rapidly following the building of the harbour in 1908.

scenes.caption: Photo 1930
scenes.text: It worsened in 1961 following construction of the Nangbeto Dam and deep-water port of Cotonou.

scenes.caption: Photo 1930
scenes.text: The official city proper population was 679,012 in 2012; however, over two million people live in the larger urban area.

scenes.title: The place
scenes.text: The wharf, an iron pier built in 1891-1893, was for decades the only sea gate of Dahomey, until the deep-water port opened in 1965.
